transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you too. Um, well, the main reason I’m here today is that I am just really, really struggling at work. I'm a registered nurse, and on the floor, I just lose my train of thought constantly. It’s gotten so severe. 

Like, I’ll be right in the middle of figuring out a really complicated patient flow issue—which takes a lot of mental coordination, you know, because you're juggling discharges and new admissions and trying to figure out bed placements and who needs what—and then the slightest thing will happen. An IV pump will start beeping a few doors down, or I'll just overhear someone asking another nurse a random question at the nurses' station, or a call light goes off in one of the rooms... and suddenly, I’ve completely forgotten what I was working on. 

The whole plan I was just holding in my head is just gone. It's like my brain just completely drops whatever I was doing the second there's any other noise or activity. And then I'm just standing there, staring at the computer or my clipboard, trying to retrace my steps to figure out what patient I was even thinking about, and it's just so incredibly frustrating because hospitals are never quiet, you know? There is always a beep or a question or an alarm. So this is happening to me all shift long, every single day, over and over, and I just feel like I'm constantly having to start my tasks over from scratch...
Have you struggled with this kind of distractibility and difficulty staying on task since you were a child, or is this a relatively new problem for you?

Oh, gosh, no, it's definitely not new. It's... it's really been a thing my entire life, honestly. I mean, going all the way back to when I was just a little kid. I remember, even in elementary school—like, second or third grade—my teachers were always, always writing the exact same things on my report cards. Every single time, it was like, "She's very bright, she has so much potential, but she's just so careless." Or, "She's not applying herself." And it wasn't that I didn't care, it was just that I was constantly, and I mean constantly, losing my worksheets. I'd do them, or half do them, and then they'd just vanish into the black hole of my desk or my backpack. 

And forgetting to turn in homework? That was just a daily occurrence. I'd literally have the finished assignment crumpled up at the bottom of my bag, and when the teacher asked for it, my brain just wouldn't register that I was supposed to hand it in, or I'd get distracted by a kid sharpening a pencil and completely forget the instruction. It was so bad that my mom... oh man, my poor mom. She literally had to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night, for hours sometimes, just to keep me on track. If she got up to stir a pot on the stove or answer the phone, I'd be off in my own world, staring at the grain of the wood on the table or playing with my eraser. She had to constantly redirect me, like, "Focus, look at the math problem, write the answer." If she wasn't right there acting as my external brain, nothing would ever get done. So, yeah, this feeling of just losing the thread of what I'm supposed to be doing... it's been with me forever. It's just that now, instead of losing a spelling worksheet, I'm losing track of a patient's care plan, which is obviously a lot more terrifying.
Beyond the difficulty staying on task, do you often feel like you have a restless 'motor' inside you, or do you frequently find yourself acting or speaking without thinking first?

Um... no, actually. Not at all. I know sometimes people think of that—like the bouncing off the walls kind of thing—but that is completely not me. I don't have that... what did you call it? A restless motor? No, I never feel like I have to be moving or doing something physical. If anything, it's almost the exact opposite. 

Like, physically, I can sit perfectly still for hours. When I was a kid, like I was just saying about sitting at the kitchen table with my mom, I wasn't squirming in my chair or trying to run around the house or climb the furniture. I was just sitting there like a lump, completely zoned out, staring at the wall or the wood grain. And even now, at the hospital, when I'm at the nurses' station trying to get my charting done, I'm not fidgeting or pacing around. I'm just sitting there, frozen, but my brain is a million miles away. 

And as for speaking without thinking or acting impulsively... no, I don't really do that either. I'm actually pretty quiet, maybe even overly cautious, because I'm always so worried I've missed some crucial piece of information during report since I zone out so much. I definitely don't blurt things out or interrupt the doctors or the other nurses. Usually, I'm the one who hasn't spoken up at all because by the time I've processed what the conversation is even about and tried to gather my thoughts, everyone else has already moved on to the next topic entirely. 

So, yeah, no restless energy or blurting things out. I just... I just drift away, I guess. Like my body is sitting right there in the chair, but the pilot has completely left the cockpit, if that makes sense? It's just this heavy, foggy feeling where I'm physically present but mentally just... gone. I never feel driven to move, I just feel like I can't keep my brain in the room with me.
